newsitem.title: UK: Britain says concludes Frigg gas treaty with NorwaY.
newsitem.headline: Britain says concludes Frigg gas treaty with NorwaY.

text.p: The British and Norwegian governments have reached agreement on revisions to the treaty governing operations of the Frigg gas pipeline, Energy Minister Lord Fraser of Carmyllie announced on Thursday.

Britain and Norway have been in dispute over the pipeline for several years. The line brings gas from the Frigg field, which straddles the territorial waters of both countries, to St Fergus in Scotland.
Under the revised treaty, the pipeline can be used to transport gas from other fields located on either side of the continental shelf boundary to St Fergus.
Until now it has only been possible to move remaining hydrocarbon reserves from the Frigg field itself.
Under an inter-governmental treaty signed in 1976, Norway is only allowed to deliver gas produced at the Frigg field alone, or at one of its satellites, until the field is fully depleted.

But Frigg output has been in decline since 1992, and Norway is now left with unused capacity on the pipeline as Frigg volumes no longer fill it. It wanted to sell gas from other fields instead, although Britain has so far blocked this.

Britain and Norway also settled the principles of a Framework Agreement to facilitate laying and operating future submarine pipelines linking oil and gas infrastructure across the continental shelf boundaries, the minister's statement said.
An agreement on the main outstanding issues of the revision of the Treaty was concluded in February between Lord Fraser and Ranveig Froiland, Norwegian Energy Minister.
Thursday's announcement marks the agreement of detailed revisions to the Treaty which have now been agreed by both parties.

If Britain starts importing more Norwegian gas this year, it is still set to become a major exporter next year as the Interconnector pipeline, linking Bacton in Norfolk on the east coast and Zeebrugge in Belgium, is due to open in October 1998.
